title: What is the difference between method hiding (static) and method overriding (instance), and how does the resolution mechanism differ (compile-time reference type vs runtime object type)?
shortTitle: What is method hiding vs method overriding?
keyPoints: Overriding (instance methods): resolved at runtime based on the actual object type via vtable (dynamic dispatch)
Hiding (static methods): resolved at compile time based on the reference variable type (static binding)
Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod() calls Parent's version (hiding, no polymorphism)
Parent p = new Child(); p.instanceMethod() calls Child's version (overriding, polymorphism)
Same object, different reference type produces different static results: proof of compile-time binding
Never call static methods on instance references: it misleads developers about the binding mechanism

s1_definition.oneliner: Overriding (instance): runtime dispatch based on actual object type. Hiding (static): compile-time binding based on reference type. Overriding is polymorphism. Hiding is not polymorphism.
s1_definition.profdef:
Two different mechanisms exist for methods with the same name in parent and child.

- **Method overriding** (instance methods): the child redefines a parent's instance method. Resolution at runtime: the JVM checks the actual object type in the heap and dispatches via the vtable. `Account ref = new SavingsAccount()` followed by `ref.getDescription()` calls SavingsAccount's version.
- **Method hiding** (static methods): the child defines a static method with the same signature as the parent's static method. Resolution at compile time: the compiler checks the variable type (reference type) and binds to that class's static method. `Account ref = new SavingsAccount()` followed by `ref.getPolicy()` calls Account's version.
- **Hiding is not polymorphism**: no dynamic dispatch occurs. The child's static method simply shadows the parent's in the child's namespace.
- **Proof**: same object, different reference type produces different static results.
s1_definition.analogy: Overriding: Rajesh calls the customer service number at National Bank of India. The system checks his actual account type at runtime and routes to the SavingsAccount team. Same number, different handler based on who is calling. Hiding: the bank's website shows the standard policy page. If you navigate to the Savings Division's website, you see their policy page. But if you use the main bank URL (parent reference), you always see the main page. The website does not check your account type.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Account ref = new SavingsAccount();

  INSTANCE METHOD (overriding)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ref.getDescription()                │
  │         │                            │
  │  Compile: Account has method? Yes.   │
  │  Runtime: actual type? SavingsAccount│
  │         │                            │
  │         ▼                            │
  │  SavingsAccount.getDescription()     │
  │  "Savings Account (4% interest)"     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  STATIC METHOD (hiding)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ref.getPolicy()                     │
  │         │                            │
  │  Compile: ref type? Account.         │
  │  Binds to Account.getPolicy()        │
  │  No runtime check.                   │
  │         │                            │
  │         ▼                            │
  │  Account.getPolicy()                 │
  │  "Standard Banking Policy"           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Method overriding applies to instance methods and uses runtime dispatch: the JVM checks the actual object type in the heap and calls the correct version. Account ref = new SavingsAccount() followed by ref.getDescription() calls SavingsAccount's version because the JVM dispatches based on the actual type. Method hiding applies to static methods and uses compile-time binding: the compiler looks at the reference variable type and binds directly. ref.getPolicy() calls Account's version because the compiler sees ref is declared as Account and never checks the actual object.

The proof: same object, different reference type produces different static results. Account ref = sa followed by ref.getPolicy() returns Standard Banking Policy. SavingsAccount saRef = sa followed by saRef.getPolicy() returns Savings Special Policy. The object did not change. Only the reference type changed. This proves static methods bind at compile time to the reference type. Instance methods bind at runtime to the actual object type.

Remember one sentence: instance methods are overridden (runtime dispatch to actual type), static methods are hidden (compile-time binding to reference type), and calling static methods on instance references is a code smell.
